The F-35 - A Signature Program Historical Background The F-35 Lightning II (Figure 29T h e F - 3 5 ), born from the Joint Strike Fighter (JSF) initiative, is among the DoD’s most ambitious acquisition programs and a centerpiece of U.S. airpower modernization. Conceived as a fifth-generation aircraft family, it was designed to deliver stealthy, multirole fighters that could replace a wide range of aging platforms across the U.S. services and close allies, while using commonality such as shared parts, software, training, and support, to reduce long-term operating costs. This strategic logic took shape in the post–Cold War period, when the U.S. and its partners confronted a dual challenge: large, aging tactical fighter inventories and tightening budgets that made separate, bespoke replacement programs for each service increasingly untenable. Rather than building three wholly distinct aircraft for the Air Force, Navy, and Marine

Hardware is still essential, but software increasingly determines whether it delivers a decisive effect. This reality underpins the emerging High-Low strategy: scalable, attritable systems (like UA Vs) complement high-end assets (like F-35s), with their synergy driven by command, control, and data. Workers from more deprived backgrounds are less likely to move to areas with higher wages, meaning that regional inequalities can perpetuate differences in income across generations. Spatial inequalities also lead to disparities in the environments in which children grow up. International evidence shows that this notably affects earnings in adulthood, with disadvantaged children achieving better outcomes if they grow up in mixed-income environments, rather than areas of concentrated deprivation. In the UK, mobility is lower in areas of greater deprivation, with the exception of some parts of London. Measures such as increased investment in transport infrastructure could help to increase growth in urban areas in the north of England which have lower levels of mobility. At a more local level, international evidence indicates that regeneration programs aimed at creating mixed-income communities improve outcomes for the children of lower-income residents. We find this leads to more stable identification of regimes and therefore use this process to backtest the implications of each regime for FX. The model suggests markets have generally oscillated between the B and E regimes in the last nine months due to a dovish-leaning Fed. However, markets traded in the T regime in May as expectations for the Fed have shifted to reflect the risk of hikes in Q4 after the more balanced rhetoric from officials, continued upside surprises in US activity and employment data, and persistent inflationary pressures. We now expect the Fed to hike at three consecutive meetings starting in December 2026, and we think the market has more space to price this in. As such, we think the number of instances in which the market trades in the T regime has scope to rise. To be clear, the overall backdrop is still very much aligned with an E regime. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 08 Jun 2026 11:20:14 ET │ 15 pages US Economics Inflation Weekly – Cleveland vs Dallas vs New York vs San Fran CITI'S TAKE Our final forecast is for a 0.22%MoM increase in May core CPI, but with details again leading to a stronger 0.37% increase in core PCE. As reaccelerating core PCE diverges from other core measures, focus will continue to shift towards the “correct” way to measure underlying inflation. Dallas Fed trimmed mean PCE at 2.3% is the lowest among alternative measures and may understate underlying inflation. But we would caution that many other measures that are now closer to 3% were also above 2% pre-pandemic. Many of these continue to gradually ease and are only 0.2- 0.5pp away from their levels in 2019, when the Fed cut rates from 2.50% to 1.75% while the unemployment rate was 3.7%. Even with three months of stronger job growth, the unemployment rate stable at 4.3% and slowing wage growth suggests the labor market is not retightening and is not a source of inflationary pressure. Almost a decade of energy under-investment has pushed the oil industry to more than halve its resource life since 2014 Under-investment in oil, an increasing focus on returns, de-leveraging, free cash flow, operational efficiency and ongoing capital discipline have taken a toll on oil resource life. According to our analysis, the resource life of Top Projects (recoverable resources/production) more than halves in 2026E from c.55 years in 2012. Yet the economics are much healthier even under lower Brent and gas price assumptions, with c.80% of the undeveloped resources profitable at a Brent price <US$70/bl vs. only 25% in 2014, on our estimates (ex). In our view, this is symptomatic of this new ‘ Age of Restraint’, with the market placing low value on undeveloped resources due to a high risk premium, and with the value accruing to the companies that can self-finance the development and manage their risk through a large diversified portfolio with benefits of scale. The largest reduction in resource life has been experienced by NOCs over the past 10 years, while Big Oils have shown a more consistent pattern over the past decade. records.text: European Economic Comment8 June 2026 ab 2 What to expect from the inflation forecast As usual, the conditional inflation forecast should be viewed as the main guidance tool (for a detailed discussion see the focus article in our September 2025 Switzerland quarterly). The main elements to watch are the end-point in Q1 2029 and the slope of the forecast. We expect the SNB to revise up its oil price assumption and also take into account the slight weakening of the CHF. records.text: ab 8 June 2026 Global Research European Economic Comment SNB: What to expect on 18 June We expect no policy rate change on 18 June We firmly expect the SNB to keep the policy rate at 0% at its upcoming meeting on 18 June (market pricing 0bp of hikes). However, if the ECB were to hike rates in the week before (on 11 June) - as we also firmly expect - the SNB may be faced with questions in the press conference whether it would also consider a tightening of its policy stance. Against this backdrop, the key objective for the SNB at the June meeting, in our view, will be to reiterate once more that the impact of the Middle East conflict on the SNB differs from other central banks - and in particular the ECB - and that the 2022 playbook (when the SNB hiked rates quickly and forcefully) should not be mechanically applied today. First, the starting point for inflation is low (0.6% in May) and remains well below the mid-point of the target range. Second, the weight of energy in the Swiss CPI is half of that in the Eurozone and electricity pricing is regulated, implying less upward pressure from higher energy prices. Third, and most important, the SNB faces not just an energy price shock but also disinflationary pressures from CHF strength, with labour market slack leaving the economy vulnerable to downside growth risks. records.text: The Impact of the World Cup on the US Economy The 2026 FIFA World Cup will take place in the US, Mexico, and Canada from June 11 to July 19. An estimated 5-6 million fans will attend 78 matches in the US. More matches will occur in June, but the audience for each match is likely to be much larger during the knockout stage that mostly occurs in July. As Exhibit 1 shows, the matches in the US will be hosted by 11 metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) that together account for roughly one third of US GDP and one quarter of US employment and the CPI index. In this week’s Analyst, we draw on historical data from the 1994 US World Cup, two decades of Super Bowls, and the Summer Olympic Games held in Los Angeles (1984), Atlanta (1996), and Salt Lake City (2002) to estimate the tournament’s impact on upcoming economic data releases, including payrolls, retail sales, consumer spending, GDP , and CPI and PCE inflation. The economic effects of major sporting events tend to be short-lived, largely reversing in the months following the event. Even so, knowing the rough size of these effects will be important for distinguishing temporary World Cup-related distortions from shifts in underlying economic trends in the months ahead. records.text: the global landscape of defense innovation. While the U.S. defense industry has historically led the way in drone technology, exemplified by the MQ-9 Reaper drone which was first deployed in the Afghanistan war in 2007, the market has since evolved dramatically. Today, consumer and commercial platforms, which are often repurposed for military use, dominate the field, as vividly demonstrated during the Russia-Ukraine war and during the current conflict between U.S./Israeli versus Iran. During the course of the Ukrainian war, First Person View (FPV) drones, Quadcopters such as the DJI Mavic 3, and others built with commercially available components have been widely deployed by both Russia and Ukraine. Despite the U.S.’s early innovation advantage in drone technology, China has emerged as the preeminent producer of low-cost, dual-use drones, leveraging its formidable manufacturing capacity and supply chain. In response to these shifts, the U.S. government has launched several initiatives to strengthen domestic drone manufacturing. The Drone Dominance Initiative, introduced in June 2025 with a $1.1 billion investment, aims to bolster the U.S. drone industry. This and similar programs like the Replicator Initiative that aims to field swarms of affordable autonomous attritable drones across air, land, and sea to counter China’s military modernization, have accelerated the development of platforms such as SpektreWorks’ LUCAS drones, now available for military procurement. The Defense Innovation Unit selected four companies, including Anduril Industries, to develop prototype solutions for flight demonstration. Remarkably, within just seven months, Anduril refined its Barracuda-500 missile design and successfully conducted a flight test (Figure 30T h e B a r r a c u d a 5 0 0 ). This achievement underscores how Barracuda’s simple, modular architecture accelerates the development, testing, and deployment of disruptive capabilities for warfighters. The Barracuda missile family—including the -100, -250, and -500 variants—embodies air-breathing, autonomous vehicles engineered for high- rate production and modular payload integration, setting a new standard for agility and scalability in defense manufacturing. A key difference we have been flagging between now and 2022 is the wage backdrop. Going into 2022, wage growth was picking up sharply. Combined with Covid-era supply dis- ruptions and tight labour supply, this drove inflation higher and forced central banks into aggressive rate hikes. Higher oil prices will mechanically push up inflation and we have already seen US headline CPI tick higher. But it is not obvious that central banks need to hike rates in response to what is essentially a demand-destructive shock. Our medium- term view is still that yields are more likely to head lower. Against that backdrop, we see an opportunity in the low-vola- tility trade: prior underperformance has created a better entry point, the setup should hold up across a wide range of macro outcomes, and it does not depend on market direction. China’s primary advantage lies in its Military-Civil Fusion (MCF) strategy. Unlike the U.S., where the commercial and defense sectors are largely distinct with a buyer-vendor relationship, China’s DIB is physically and operationally entwined with its global manufacturing base. China’s MCF promotes deep integration between its defense and civilian industries. The MCF ensures that new innovations simultaneously advance economic and military development by removing barriers between China’s civilian and commercial sectors and its military and defense industrial sectors. For example, commercially available Chinese DJI drones have been deployed in the Ukraine-Russia war with great effectiveness. German fiscal spending has been weak so far, but the pipeline is building German infrastructure spending has disappointed in the early stages. Through April, only €11 billion of the €40 billion ear- marked for 2026 has been deployed (roughly 28% of the annual allocation). Last year was similar with authorities spending €24 billion of a planned €37 billion. The shortfalls span across broadband expansion, rail network upgrades and broader transport infrastructure. The shortfall occurred mainly because the planning process is lengthy, bureaucracy is entrenched, and the 2025 election cycle delayed the legislative framework from taking effect until late last year. However, these are now being addressed. Merz's government has introduced fast-track legislation for projects of overriding public interest, and the Finance Minis- try has explicitly urged departments to accelerate disburse- ments. As such, the prevalence of instances where the market trades in the “T regime” has scope to rise. To be clear, this is not a decisive and permanent shift. The backdrop overall is still aligned with an “E regime”, especially given the constructive outlook for equities and credit. Rather, we think markets can transition from trading some combination of the B/E regimes to now the E/T regimes. This has important implications for the USD. On each given day, we blend data by adding the total quoted amount in the order book from both sources for each displayed currency pair. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. For example, a 90th percentile reading for EURUSD indicates that the current depth of book value is ranked in the top 10% of historical observations over the last year. Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. Prior to July 2020, we aggregate total traded volume from EBS with estimated trading volume from Reuters, which is calculated as a product of total paid-given count and average trade size. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. The deal is headline-grabbing, but more importantly from a flows perspective, it will be a call on liquidity. It comes at a time of very strong wealth effects f or US retail investors, driven in part by robust recent gains in S emis. Rule changes for prominent equity indices have also fueled headlines about large potential passive buying flows. This implies significant selling elsewhere. IPOs have often exhibited high volatility and fat tails. With the confluence of flows expected around SpaceX’s flotation, we think this time will not be an exception. What is unprecedented is that volatility in this stock will be coupled with the largest m arket cap ever seen in a US IPO. Typically, Fed rate hikes lead to an increase in foreign investor buying of USD assets that are FX unhedged due to the higher hedging cost. Our revised call for three 25bp Fed rate hikes and two 25bp ECB hikes over the next 12 months would see the cost for a eurozone investor to FX hedge USD assets rise approximately 50bp from around 1.5% currently to 2.0% over the next year. However, we think USD buying through this channel will be weaker this time than in past Fed-tightening episodes. Foreign investor holdings of FX-unhedged USD assets remain close to historical highs, which suggests there’s less room for these holdings to increase compared with past Fed-tightening episodes. Where data is available for eurozone investors (e.g. Dutch and Danish pension funds), we find FX-unhedged USD asset holdings have fallen as a proportion of total assets since the start of 2025 but they’re still at the top end of the historical range. records.text: M Idea 6 Based on past speeches by the Governor and analyses of underlying inflation and the neutral rate published under the Monetary Affairs Department’s name, the Department—which plays a leading role in shaping policy discussions at the staff level —appears to be developing a rate-hike rationale that contemplates policy rates above 1.0% (BoJ Watch: Our Take on BoJ’s Recent Communications: Underlying Inflation, Neutral Rate, Summary of Opinions, and Other (31 Mar 2026)). In this context, it is natural that policy discussions led by the Department are oriented toward further rate hikes. That said, in assessing the need for further tightening, the first key issue is which factors the BoJ places greater weight on in assessing the strengthening of underlying inflation. Namely, attention should be paid to whether greater emphasis is placed on (i) upward pressure on prices stemming from “second-round effects” triggered by higher crude oil prices or (ii) a strengthening in underlying inflation driven by factors closer to fundamentals, such as stronger wage-to-price pass-through. In particular, the fact that a stronger wage-to-price pass-through was not clearly evident in April price revisions remains an important issue, and it will be important to assess whether the BoJ fine-tunes its policy discussion on this point and what policy implications may lie behind such fine-tuning. records.text: TRADE IDEA TRADE IDEA 09/06/2026 1 FX: Exit long USDPEN We exit our long USDPEN 1m NDF position, booking a loss of 3.1% (USD156k). The market’s assessment that Keiko Fujimori would win the runoff—based largely on the offshore vote count that skewed in her favor—prompted a rapid slide in the USDPEN. The risk premium that had accrued after the initial count has now been stripped away, even though the final outcome is still pending. In fact, with election-related bearish pressure now gone, our STEER fair-value model flags the PEN as the most overvalued currency in the region. To recap, we initiated the position on 5 June because we believed that the low election-related risk premium priced in to local assets, coupled with already sizable net-long positions and potential profit-taking after the runoff, had created a negatively asymmetric risk profile in the wake of the election. We also felt that May’s strong US NFP had skewed risks toward an upward move in USDPEN (see FX: Long USDPEN on election uncertainty). If these gaps are not closed, the U.S. risks both failing to deter adversaries, who increasingly read American industrial constraints as a window of opportunity, and losing future conflicts in which the side that iterates, regenerates, and adapts fastest holds the decisive edge. Institutional change is building momentum: the FY26 NDAA’s commercial-first provisions, expanded use of Other Transaction Agreements, MOSA, and software- appropriate acquisition pathways all point in the right direction. But operational follow- through is far from assured. Procurement reform can be undone by PPBE rigidity, IP and data-rights disputes, compliance culture, and the gravitational pull of legacy incentives. Both the institutional and productive challenges remain tall, and they are deeply intertwined, resolving the former is a precondition for delivering on the latter. The next few years will determine whether America’s defense industrial base evolves into the integrated, scalable, software-driven enterprise the moment requires, or whether reform stalls in the practical mechanics of funding, contracting, and execution. records.text: M Idea 8 Hawkish Surprise Unlikely Koichi Sugisaki, Hiromu Uezato (Japan Macro Strategy team) JPY Rates: BoJ’s Hawkish Communication Already Priced In Markets have already priced in a high probability—over 90%—of a rate hike at the June meeting, following Governor Ueda’s speech at the Kisaragi-kai on the June 3rd and subsequent media reports. As such, the decision to raise rates itself is unlikely to come as a surprise. Instead, market focus will shift to Governor Ueda’s press conference, particularly his communication regarding upside inflation risks and concerns about falling behind the curve. The key message from the June 3 speech was moderately hawkish. In essence, while higher oil prices could weigh on economic activity, the BoJ is placing greater emphasis on upside risks to inflation at this stage. Notably, even with prolonged Middle East tensions, the Bank clarified its stance of adjusting the degree of monetary accommodation in a tightening direction, provided that the economy does not deteriorate significantly. Downside risks to the economy are viewed as limited, supported by resilient corporate earnings, wage increases following the spring wage negotiations, and government energy relief measures that should prevent a sharp deterioration in private consumption. In contrast, upside inflation risks are seen as more significant, underpinned by rising inflation expectations and recent increases in corporate goods prices, with a heightened risk of second-round effects. Earlier, Tenaris consolidated the US shale OCTG market through the acquisition of TMK’s US assets (IPSCO) in 2020, which led to the removal of a key competitor in premium seamless. In parallel, Vallourec exited commodity markets and permanently closed high‑cost European mills, concentrating production in Brazil, the US and China, while TMK is now a regional CIS player following sanctions and the loss of Western premium market access. Industry structure has also tightened through “virtual consolidation” driven by trade policy and technology barriers. US steel tariffs (Section 232), raised to up to 50% on certain imports in 2025, have effectively regionalised the market, leading to foreign players localising capacity or exiting the market. As a result, OCTG has shifted from a volume‑driven global market to a premium, regionally protected structure dominated by vertically integrated producers. Pricing power increasingly rests on proprietary premium connections (TenarisHydril, VAM), now a prerequisite for complex US shale and deepwater wells, rather than tube capacity alone. The combined effects of M&A, capacity exits and trade protection have materially tightened the Tier‑1 landscape, reinforcing capital discipline and supporting structurally higher margins despite rig count cyclicality. records.text: Noel Dixon 08 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General BoC Preview : Hold and See Since the Bank of Canada’s last policy meeting, Canada’s outlook has become more uncertain. The economy slipped into a technical recession in Q1 and now faces two major risks: the US-Iran war and the USMCA review starting July 1. Even so, early signs of recovery are emerging in the labour market and consumer spending, while inflation, though rising, remains relatively contained. Taken together, these conditions suggest the BoC can afford to remain patient. We therefore expect it will hold rates steady at its June 10th meeting and stress the need for more evidence on how the economy evolves. Our Hawkish-Dovish Index now ranks the BoC as the most dovish central bank in the G10. Given that stance and the added uncertainty around the USMCA review, we are downgrading our medium-term view on the CAD from positive to neutral pending greater clarity. Still, we believe the recovery is taking hold and that much of the bad news is already priced in, so we are not turning fully negative on the currency at current levels. Canada’s economy unexpectedly entered a technical recession in Q1. Final domestic demand also fell 0.4% QoQ SAAR, indicating the weakness was broad-based rather than superficial. What most differentiates the F-35 is the architecture of its mission systems. Its signature capability is sensor fusion, the integration of radar, infrared, and electronic warfare inputs into a single, coherent operational picture intended to reduce pilot workload and accelerate decisions. This is reinforced by 360-degree situational awareness, enabled by distributed sensors (often described as a Distributed Aperture System), allowing detection and tracking across all aspects of the battlefield. The aircraft is also designed for network-centric operations, sharing and receiving near real-time information with other platforms and forces, which extends its role beyond delivering weapons to acting as an airborne node in a joint and coalition kill chain. Finally, internal weapons bays are central to the F-35’s survivability concept, enabling weapons carriage while preserving low observability compared to external stores. Alternatively, is the target considered consistent if underlying inflation averages 2% with some fluctuations, meaning temporary overshoots are permissible? While it may have been premature to discuss these points before, now is the time for a full-fledged debate, as the BoJ anticipates reaching a state consistent with the target from the second half of fiscal 2026 onwards. This issue is important for understanding the asymmetry of the policy reaction function. In the past, during the process of exiting deflation, a deliberate "behind- the-curve" strategy while underlying inflation was below 2% had a certain rationale, as it helped push inflation toward 2%. However, now that Governor Ueda has clearly signaled his concern about the risk of "getting behind the curve," we should consider this policy stance as having already shifted. We believe that once underlying inflation reaches 2%, or even when its path toward 2% becomes foreseeable, a similar strategy would risk an inflation overshoot and threaten the achievement of the "price stability target." In other words, we understand that the BoJ's policy reaction function is changing to become more forward-looking as inflation approaches 2%, and the need to respond more swiftly to upside risks is increasing. After ending QT earlier than expected last fall, the Fed unexpectedly restarted asset purchases with its Reserve Management Purchase (RMP) Program. This program quickly ramped up to $40B+ / month in the name of financial market stability. However, even after funding markets stabilized, the program continued unabated perhaps as a means of soaking up incremental T Bill supply from the Treasury. All in, the RMP and ending of QT has added approximately $250B of liquidity since the end of the year. Second, the Fed lowered capital requirements for the banks via the SLR. This effectively increased the capital available to buy Treasuries or to make new loans by almost $200B. Finally, the Treasury upped its Treasury buyback program in March to record levels, targeting back end supply. They bought $125B of Treasuries over a 6-week period starting in early March which was quite effective in reducing bond volatility after the sharp spike in March from rising oil prices and the repricing of Fed cuts. Lower bond vol essentially increases the collateral in the banking system and financial markets. All three of these activities have far surpassed most expectations at the beginning of the year and helped support the powerful rallies in various commodity markets discussed above. An Indo-Pacific fight would likely force U.S. and allied aircraft to operate from more distant bases due to missile threats to forward airfields, carriers, and tankers. This increases the F-35’s dependence on aerial refueling and distributed basing; if tankers are degraded or pushed back, combat reach, persistence, and sortie rates fall. Second, the F-35’s edge depends on connectivity. Its core advantage comes from sensor fusion and data sharing, but a peer adversary can attack the enabling networks through EW, cyber, and anti- satellite actions. Under a rules-based regime, tariff changes were infrequent and predictable. Under a discretionary regime, policy can respond rapidly to political and industrial priorities, raising the risk of renewed tariff shocks and second-round effects on prices. records.text: keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 208/06/2026 Although the Middle East crisis prompted the government to lower its growth forecast for this year from 1.0% to 0.9%, the budget deficit target has been retained at 5% of GDP. At this stage we believe there are solid arguments for still considering that target credible Favourable base effects help: Last year’s 5.1% deficit undershot the 5.4% target, and while the government attributed about 0.2% of that gap to a one-off factor, there is a slight favourable base effect of 0.1% of GDP linked to last year’s spending cuts. Monthly central government data still points to a better-than-expected trend over the first four months of the year. At end-April the deficit was roughly flat versus a year earlier (Figure 5). This compares with expectations in the 2026 budget law for a EUR10bn deterioration in the central government budget. Growth underlying resilience: Activity was weaker than expected in Q1: GDP growth was −0.1% q/q (our forecast +0.3%) and falling business sentiment scores across surveys have increased the risk of a further contraction in activity (Figure 15). Negative one-off factors were partly to blame for the poor Q1 GDP number. Construction suffered from adverse weather conditions and the decline in exports and investment in Q1 was largely driven by a slump in the transport sector, especially in aeronautics, which appears disconnected from otherwise relatively resilient business sentiment

High inflation in recent years has made it harder to draw out the activity increase in volume terms. The INSEE has just revised up its assessment of the 2023 and 2024 trend, and we think revisions to 2025 should not be excluded. Given the lag, however, this will not be known before next year at the earliest. The revisions suggest the value-added from French industry end of 2025 was around 5% above the previous estimate, and therefore about 3% above pre-Covid levels (Figure 11). They also suggest that among the main eurozone countries, France experienced one of the strongest industrial recovery post Covid (Figure 12). French GDP growth was thus revised up for 2023 and 2024, to 1.9% and 1.4% respectively (from 1.6% and 1.1% previously) (Figure 13). records.text: Offshore construction and EPCI: Since 2014, the offshore construction and EPCI industry has undergone a deep structural consolidation, which led to the number of Tier‑1 contractors capable of executing complex deepwater and SURF (Subsea, Umbilicals, Risers, and Flowlines) projects falling from 9 players to 7 today. The first phase focused on vertical integration, most notably the creation of TechnipFMC in 2017 through the merger of Technip and FMC Technologies, which established the first fully integrated subsea provider. This period also saw unsuccessful consolidation efforts and exits, including EMAS Chiyoda Subsea entering Chapter 11 in 2017 and the McDermott-Chicago Bridge & Iron Company (CB&I) combination in 2018. The second phase (2019-24) was marked by de‑leveraging and specialization: TechnipFMC spun off Technip Energies in 2021, while McDermott divested CB&I’s storage business in December 2024 for US$475m. CB&I subsequently became a debt‑free standalone entity. The final super consolidation phase could occur in 2026 and reshape the competitive landscape. In July 2025, Saipem and Subsea 7 agreed to merge Saipem’s Offshore E&C business with Subsea 7; the acquisition is expected to close in 2H26 and would consolidate two of Europe’s largest offshore contractors into a single leading player. (↔) Debate among Fed officials and market participants is quickly shifting towards the correct way to measure underlying inflation, as a reacceleration of core PCE back above 3% is an outlier among other inflation measures (core CPI, alternative measures). This debate becomes more important in the context of core PCE experiencing measurement issues related to AI-affected components. Dallas Fed President Logan spoke last week on the stickiness of core inflation, downplaying her own Fed’s trimmed mean PCE which stands at just 2.3%. Dallas Fed researchers have highlighted recently that because the trimmed mean excludes more strong components than weak components, it may be too soft in periods where more prices are rising relative to prices that are falling. The Dallas measure trims the weakest components comprising 24% of the weight of core PCE but excludes the strongest 31% (by weight) of components. Logan instead highlighted other underlying inflation measures that remain closer to 3%, such as the Cleveland Fed’s median PCE. Unlike the Dallas trimmed mean, which excludes different shares of too-weak or too-strong prices, median PCE reflects the price of the component at the 50th percentile weight in a distribution of ~200 components of PCE. As of April, Cleveland median PCE was at 2.8%. But importantly, both Dallas and Cleveland measures have both been trending consistently lower, in opposition to core PCE. Cleveland media

records.text: Brazil and UAE support peak non-OPEC production growth in 2027, decelerating in 2028 We expect non-OPEC (ex-Russia, ex-US shale) supply growth to moderate over the medium term, despite a near-term peak in project-driven volumes. Importantly, the UAE’s exit from OPEC in April 2026 shifts a material source of growth into the non-OPEC bucket, mechanically boosting reported supply additions from 2027 onwards. Based on our database, assuming a c.5% underlying decline rate, the system requires c.1mb/d of new production annually to keep non-OPEC, ex-shale oil production output flat; against this, we forecast c.1.4mb/d of supply additions in 2027, before moderating to c.1mb/d in 2028 and 500-600kb/d in 2029-30, implying a gradual tightening in underlying balances. Looking at project-level contributions, growth is increasingly concentrated in a limited number of large-scale developments, led by Búzios (Brazil, +810kb/d by 2030 vs 2025), Stabroek (Guyana, +600kb/d), and Upper Zakum expansion (UAE, +500kb/d), alongside Argentina shale (+700kb/d), Tilenga/Kingfisher (Uganda, +200kb/d), Block 58 (Suriname, +200kb/d) and Bacalhau (Brazil, +200kb/d). In addition, we see a meaningful contribution from associated liquids linked to gas projects, notably NGLs from US shale (+1.4 mb/d by 2030), Jafurah field in Saudi Arabia (+600-700 kb/d) and Qatar North Field East LNG (+238kb/d). USD performance around can be broken into two distinct segments: the expectations period and after the delivery. The expectations period has historically always proven USD positive, with the dollar trading strongly in line with the rise in front end yields. The delivery itself results in more mixed USD performance. Previously when the Fed hiked interest rates, on average the USD rallies 4% in the 6m leading to that meeting. The US 2y yield rises by on average 80bp in this period. The market has already priced in the risk of a hike in December, with about 35bp of hikes embedded in the curve until mid-2027. This may be too low. We think that if the Fed were to deliver hikes, then 1999 is the closest analog to today given how in both cases the Fed delivered insurance cuts but then was met by an unexpectedly strong economy. Securing the future Our broader take, however, is that the direction of travel is likely to be shaped by the following factors. First, as mentioned, the nature of war has changed and communication and control capabilities will be fundamental in the digital age. Second, that successful defense industrial bases elsewhere, each in their own way, have largely based their success on the integration of their defense and commercial industrial bases. Third, and related to the two above, that the U.S. possesses a technological edge in the digital space that sits largely in the commercial sector, and that integrating it to the defense ecosystem is crucial for the U.S. to keep its military dominance. Spending on food and beverages by foreign tourists, domestic tourists, and locals will boost retail sales, which does not distinguish between spending by residents and foreigners. USD performance during those episodes can be divided into two distinct parts: the expectations period and the post-delivery period. The expectations period has historically always proven USD positive, with the dollar trading strongly in line with the rise in front-end yields. However, the delivery of the first rate hike of a cycle results in more mixed USD performance. In previous instances of the Fed hiking rates for the first time in a cycle, the USD TWI rallied 4% in the six months leading up to that policy meeting, while the US 2y yield rose 80bp on average. If the Fed were to deliver hikes, then the conditions would be most similar to those in 1999, in our view, given how in both cases the Fed delivered insurance cuts but then encountered an unexpectedly strong economy. Our revised Fed funds call reflects this strategy and we see it three consecutive hikes starting in December 2026 to undo the easing in 2025. In 1999, the USD TWI rallied 2% as the 2y yield rose 95bp in that six-month period. We expect the BoJ to decide on an additional 0.25% rate hike, raising its target for the uncollateralized overnight call rate to around 1.00%. n The primary reason for this forecast is the strong sense of urgency Governor Ueda expressed in his June 3 speech about the risk of "getting behind the curve." The Governor explicitly stated his desire to avoid a situation where a delayed response would necessitate sharp rate hikes later. We believe this forward-looking risk management stance shortens the timeframe we had previously assumed the BoJ would take to "carefully scrutinize data," thereby increasing the probability of a preemptive rate hike. records.text: The Impact of the World Cup on the US Economy The 2026 FIFA World Cup will take place in the US, Mexico, and Canada from June 11 to July 19. An estimated 5-6 million fans will attend 78 matches in the US. More matches will occur in June, but the audience for each match is likely to be much larger during the knockout stage that mostly occurs in July. As Exhibit 1 shows, the matches in the US will be hosted by 11 metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) that together account for roughly one third of US GDP and one quarter of US employment and the CPI index. In this week’s Analyst, we draw on historical data from the 1994 US World Cup, two decades of Super Bowls, and the Summer Olympic Games held in Los Angeles (1984), Atlanta (1996), and Salt Lake City (2002) to estimate the tournament’s impact on upcoming economic data releases, including payrolls, retail sales, consumer spending, GDP , and CPI and PCE inflation. The economic effects of major sporting events tend to be short-lived, largely reversing in the months following the event. Even so, knowing the rough size of these effects will be important for distinguishing temporary World Cup-related distortions from shifts in underlying economic trends in the months ahead. Impact on Payrolls Payroll employment rose 80k above trend in host cities during the 1994 US World Cup and 40k on average during past Summer Olympics in the event months, before largely reverting to trend in the following months (Exhibit 2). The future path of JGB purchases influences ASW valuations mainly through shifts in expectations around supply-demand conditions. However, as discussed in “Japan | Detail about underlying our updated JGB yield forecasts,” even if the purchase amount is maintained—or further reduced—beyond April 2027, the impact on the fair value of ASWs within the sub-10-year sector is likely to be limited (see Exhibit 11 ). Rather, outcomes will depend more heavily on how the MoF adjusts issuance across maturities. For 10y+ sectors, the overall scale of purchases is small to begin with, suggesting limited impact on ASW fair value here as well (see Exhibit 12 ). Instead, investor demand dynamics and the potential for additional issuance cuts by the MoF are likely to be more consequential.

records.text: In this report we focus on earnings mobility. But studies also highlight that differences in wealth show a strong tendency to persist across generations – partly as a result of increases in house prices – indicating that this is an important area for future research. Growth Upside A majority of the British public thinks that more should be done to promote equal opportunity, highlighting that improving social mobility is an important objective in its own right. But increased social mobility would also likely result in economic gains, through two channels. First, improving the allocation of talent across occupations should increase efficiency, and recent research has found that this could provide a moderate boost to the level of UK productivity. It is true that another report using Swedish data finds only a marginal impact on aggregate earnings, but this may understate the effect given that Sweden has high social mobility and research has found the allocation of talent to be very important in other contexts. Second, international evidence suggests that high-ability children from poorer backgrounds are much less likely to become inventors later in life than those from wealthier families. Allowing these “lost Einsteins and Marie Curies” to fulfill their potential could boost innovation and generate a persistent increase in productivity growth. P/B relatives (10%) – P/B versus own history, normalised. Lower z scores = cheaper, more favourable. 3. Earnings revisions (20%) – Average of 1 month and 3 month earnings revisions, normalised. Higher z scores = improving earnings expectations. 4. Forward EPS change (20%) – Average of 1 month, 3 month and 12-month EPS changes, normalised (1.25x weighting if all three are positive). Higher z scores = improving earnings growth. 5. UBS crowding (5%) – Crowded longs score positively. After normalisation, lower (more negative) z scores = more contrarian, more favourable. 6. Analyst recommendations (5%) – Scale from 1 (buy) to 5 (sell), normalised. Higher z scores imply more bearish consensus and are treated as a contrarian positive. 7. Price momentum (20%) – Average of 1-month, 3 month relative performance, and 12 month relative performance (all vs MSCI ACWI), normalised (1.25x weighting if all three are positive). Higher z scores = stronger momentum. 8. ROE over ROE volatility (10%) – Profitability stability measure, normalised. Higher z scores = higher quality. In contrast, if energy prices were to trend higher again, then outside of the US, markets would have ample room to begin considering downside risks to growth after the energy-price shock. This means markets may still price in rate hikes for other central banks, but then the potential demand destruction stemming from higher energy costs and restrictive policy rates should intensify hedging for cuts soon after, in our view. In contrast, the market may be less inclined to price in downside risks to US economic growth given that the country is relatively insulated from higher energy prices. records.text: Shale goes global, as the US matures. Spotlight on Argentina and Saudi After 15 years of extraordinary growth, supplying 60% of global non-OPEC supply increase, US shale oil is reaching maturity and is starting to plateau. As energy companies start to work on shale oil opportunities outside of the USA, we spotlight two giant unconventional assets, leveraging our Top projects database: the Vaca Muerta in Argentina and the Jafurah field in Saudi Arabia, which are about to deliver material growth. We are also starting to see the early signs of a new trend for the US E&Ps going abroad with the latest examples including Continental entering into the Vaca Muerta and EOG Resources in the UAE — a clear reversal of the reshoring trend of the past decade. Overall, we estimate that the shale projects under development in Argentina and Saudi Arabia could together add c.270 kboed of annual liquids (oil and NGLs) growth to 2030, representing almost 1/5 of global annual oil demand growth, with further potential upside from other countries like the UAE. These fields will also add material gas production, propelling Argentina to become a major LNG exporter by the end of the decade and ending Saudi’s c.500 kbpd of crude oil burn for power generation by the early 2030s - signalling that shale is now ready to have a meaningful global impact outside the USA. UK—The Potential Economic Gains from Boosting Social Mobility Social mobility measures for the UK show a mixed picture. On the one hand, most British people still earn more than their parents did in an absolute sense. The UK also has a high rate of upward educational mobility – owing to the expansion of higher education in recent decades – and the Social Mobility Commission judges that rates of upward occupational mobility are in line with western European averages. At the same time, workers’ relative positions in the earnings distribution remain closely tied to those of their parents. Estimates from the OECD and World Bank suggest that the link is stronger in the UK than the average across other advanced economies.1 1 Another OECD study exploring the link between relative earnings and parental education (as opposed to parental earnings) suggests that the UK has a higher degree of mobility than the OECD average for men. That said, the report finds that mobility is lower than the OECD average for women, finds that workers with less educated parents face a notable earnings penalty and shows strong intergenerational persistence in labour market participation. We would point out that commodities often exhibit this type of volatility while still in the midst of a long bull market. For the record, we think Gold and Silver stocks remain in a robust bull market even though they are still in the midst of a correction. Regular readers will know that we view liquidity as a key (and maybe the most important) driver of the bull market since the pandemic. We have documented in great detail the relationship between stocks and Gold or other inflation proxies. Since the beginning of the year, one could argue that we have simply been rotating from one commodity to the next starting with Gold and Silver, then Metals, Energy and most recently, DRAM/Semis. It would seem to us that if Semis are now going to correct in a meaningful manner, the most important question to ask oneself is what is the next leadership asset, and will it be commodity-oriented or something else? Secondarily, our core view is that earnings remain robust, broader and more sustainable than most believe. That suggests the diversified S&P 500 can withstand another leadership change and that change is likely to happen during a correction where the new leaders go down less or not at all (Transports were up on Friday). On that basis, we will be even more focused on relative performance over the next few weeks as the equity market likely goes through this transition.

Several FOMC participants have emphasized anchored inflation expectations as a key source of the Fed's credibility, and the edge down in the FRBNY measures continues to signal well- anchored expectations, at least on this metric. On Friday, preliminary June estimates of consumer sentiment and inflation expectations will arrive from the University of Michigan, which will offer a more timely reading ahead of the FOMC meeting next week. Read our full preview of the meeting in the US Economics Weekly "Hawkish NFP , inflation week next" on page 3. In the May FRBNY survey, labor market assessments were mixed. The mean perceived probability of finding a job in the next three months if one loses a job today rose, while expectations that the unemployment rate would be higher in a year's time fell. Households continue to point to worsening financial situations on both a current and year-ahead basis with the mean probability of consumers being unable to make the minimum monthly payment rising in May. records.text: ile we acknowledge that new Chair Warsh will likely seek to avoid hiking rates in his early days of leading the Fed, our view is that regardless of who heads the central bank, monetary policy will be determined by the economic outlook and by the FOMC’s existing policy goals and strategy, in whatever direction the data leads it . In his confirmation testimony, Warsh pointed to the trimmed mean PCE measure of inflation as close to 2% . We believe the public use of this measure to argue that current elevated inflation is transitory is consistent with our expectation for rate hikes to come with a substantial delay but then to proceed sequentially to catch up. In June 2021, the Fed similarly relied on trimmed mean measures (at that point printing at 1.8%) amid the demand shock of the pandemic reopening to argue that rapidly rising inflation was driven by “special factors” and that a policy response was not required. Policy tight ening followed months later, in March 2022.

Active oil rig counts edge up for the sixth straight week Active oil drilling rigs rose by 2 to 431 in the week ending June 5 according to Baker Hughes, the sixth consecutive week of increases. Immediately following the beginning of the conflict, oil rig counts generally moved sideways, with little evidence that the run- up in oil prices had translated into more drilling. records.text: Market structure in offshore services has materially improved The oil services industry has been structurally transformed over the past decade, shifting from being a highly competitive, fragmented market with frequent new entrants to a tightly consolidated industry characterised by high barriers to entry and a limited number of global players. Offshore drilling: Since 2014, the offshore drilling industry has undergone a structural consolidation with the number of key offshore drillers falling from 15 players to 8 today (‑60%), driven by a decade‑long cycle of bankruptcies, mergers and asset transfers. Between 2016 and 2021, Valaris, Seadrill, Noble, Diamond Offshore and Pacific Drilling all filed for Chapter 11, which led to fleet rationalisation. The consolidation phase accelerated post restructuring: Transocean acquired Songa Offshore (2018) and Ocean Rig; Noble absorbed Pacific Drilling (2021), Maersk Drilling (2022) and Diamond Offshore (2024); Seadrill acquired Aquadrill (2023); ADES acquired Shelf Drilling (2025); and Transocean expects the closing of the Valaris acquisition in 2H26. As a result, modern high‑spec fleets are now concentrated among a handful of operators that control the majority of seventh‑gen drillships, harsh‑environment floaters and premium jack‑ups. Looking at how the markets traded in in 1999, the USD rallied 2% as the 2y yield rose 95bp in that 6m period. There are fundamental differences in markets at the time (the EUR had just been introduced for instance), but taking the aggregated historical episodes and 1999 episode together, this would imply that if the 2y yield today was to rise by an additional 50bp then that should contribute to 1-2.5% upside for the USD in the coming 6 months. Our bias for now is that the USD move will be towards the lower end of that range. This is because there still does remain a high bar for the market to price in an overly hawkish Fed. In addition, if markets were to indeed price in a more aggressive rate path, that may be accompanied by some hedging that a slowdown follows afterwards. Regardless, thus far the broad USD has not been strongly driven by front end rate differentials according to our STEER model, and we see scope for that to change going forward. As such, it is worth considering how the Fed being priced for a hikes aligns with expectations for other central banks. Since the start of the middle east conflict, global front end yields have risen to reflect the upside risks to inflation from higher energy prices. If there is an imminent resolution, we think that Fed hike pricing is more durable than other central banks. This is because central bank repricing elsewhere was driven by energy prices while the Fed repricing has been driven by stronger activity data. Thus, if a de-escalation contributes to broad USD weakness, we would be more amenable to using that as a “buy the dip” opportunity in the USD as rate differentials may narrow in favor of the USD. When deciding where to buy the dip, we think it would be against low yielders as markets seek to earn carry. We therefore think two conditions should be met in choosing a pair: 1) the other central bank should currently be priced for hikes and 2) it is unlikely that those hikes are ultimately delivered. USDCAD stands out here in that regard given the softer growth and steady inflation data in Canada. Our options strike map suggests light gamma positioning above the 1.39 level, suggesting risks for an acceleration higher. On fundamentals, demand -side pressures remain elevated, and the pass -through from industrial profits to actual employment change has weakened. That said, CNY is less cyclical and less prone to market shocks, with domestic weakness typically transmitted via equity flows rather than trade weakness. records.text: Fed appears to be increasingly concerned by the length of the inflation overshoot and the possibility that it may run for several more years. Other policymakers have made similar arguments in recent weeks, and we see Waller – who was earlier among the most skeptical that LTIE was at risk – as signaling an emerging sea change in the Fe d’s thinking. In JADC2 terms, this is the backbone: without robust communications, data can’t flow fast enough to drive effective action. Precision effects in Ukraine depended on space-provided PNT, but electronic warfare (EW) quickly challenged this advantage. GNSS signals were jammed and spoofed, sparking a constant contest over navigation and targeting. Ukraine, the U.S., and manufacturers adapted systems and tactics in real time, while Russia countered—proving that in an EW-rich environment, precision is a moving target, maintained through continual iteration. This underscores why JADC2 prioritizes rapid, software-enabled decision-making: when navigation, communications, and sensing are contested, the side that integrates data and adapts fastest keeps the kill chain intact. The Imperatives: Integration, Scale, and Innovation The U.S. defense-industrial enterprise now stands at a decisive inflection point. We therefore also consider a top-down estimate of the impact on GDP by estimating the effects of past Super Bowls using Gross State Product data. We then rescale the estimated effect of the Super Bowl to a World Cup effect by assuming that the ratio of the events’ GDP effects will be the same as the ratio of their cumulative effects on employment. Exhibit 5 shows that this approach implies a boost to annualized GDP growth of 0.1pp in Q2 and 0.05pp in Q3, which should then give way to a modest drag in Q4. These figures are close to but a bit larger than the bottom-up estimates above, as one would expect. High-for-longer fuel prices, however, could pressure the government to do more. Recent polls have shown strong public support for broader measures amid demands from hard-right or hard-left parties to cut fuel taxes or cap prices (Figure 7). Cutting VAT on fuel from 20% to 5.5%, as floated by Rassemblement National (RN), would cost EUR10–12bn (0.4% of GDP). Peak political pressure around fuel prices may be passing, however. The latest consumer survey showed more moderate consumer expectations for future prices. Rise of the technocrats: Because he has removed from his cabinet any ministers with presidential ambitions, we think Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is in a stronger position to face down calls for broad-based, costly fiscal support – and to stick to the budget deficit target. In our view, Lecornu’s cabinet is essentially behaving like a team of technocrats, signalling it will freeze credit lines worth more than EUR6bn (about 0.2 % of GDP) to offset the negative budget impact of weaker growth and higher interest payments. New threats; new vulnerabilities But what worked before may not work now. Today’s DIB structure exposes four compounding vulnerabilities: • Shallow production depth: Thinned ranks of tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers create bottlenecks that can stall or cripple programs. • Slow acquisition: Major defense programs drag on for eight years or more, lagging behind rapid technological shifts. • Industry concentration: A handful of dominant primes stifle competition, slow alternative production lines, and weaken system resilience. • Supply-chain fragility: Global, multi-tiered supply chains are efficient but hard to de-risk—especially with dependencies on China for critical materials and components. We expect capex spend to accelerate to 11% in 2027 Following a period of moderation in 2025-26, we expect global upstream capex to reaccelerate, with our updated database pointing to 11% growth in 2027 and 6% in 2028. This inflection is driven by a pickup in project sanctioning, with offshore capex growth accelerating to 6% in 2027 and 10% in 2028, consistent with the lagged impact of the deepwater FID cycle. Within offshore, growth is led by deepwater, where we forecast capex increasing by 5%/15%/ 6% in 2027-29, outpacing shallow-water developments. In contrast, LNG capex spend remains supportive in 2027 (+16%) but begins to slow from 2028 onwards, reflecting the peak and subsequent deceleration in LNG FIDs. At the same time, US shale remains a steady growth contributor, with c.10% capex growth in 2027 and mid-single-digit growth thereafter. Industry commentary points to a measured activity recovery, with Diamondback highlighting potential for a 10-15% increase in Permian rigs, albeit with a slower response than in prior cycles given consolidation and capital discipline, while Tenaris expects the US rig count to increase by c.50 rigs (c.+10%) by year-end. This raises the risk of a fresh round of price increases from autumn. The shift is also evident in the analysis. Re-estimating the VAR using data since 2015, the CPI response to a 10% rise in oil prices is about 1.5 times larger (Exhibit 7). This suggests that the current roughly 50% oil price shock could lift CPI by around 2ppt. Longer term, inflation expectations are key CPI is likely to reaccelerate following the current oil shock. As a temporary supply shock, the medium-term outlook depends on how inflation expectations among firms and households respond. Our BofA inflation expectations indicator shows that expectations, after falling during COVID, rose sharply following the Ukraine shock and subsequent inflation pickup, and have continued to rise. strial ecosystem. • Second, foreign dependency. Even where final assembly occurs domestically, the U.S. defense supply chain is tightly interwoven with global industrial networks, and in many instances is directly exposed to dependencies linked to China. Raw materials, processed inputs, and specialized manufacturing steps are frequently sourced abroad. These dependencies create acute risks: strategic disruption becomes plausible, either through geopolitical coercion, export controls, market manipulation, or simple supply chain shocks. Substituting these foreign supply sources is not a simple fix; it requires recertification, qualification, and navigating the same slow- moving acquisition logic that created the vulnerabilities to begin with. • Third, the production throughput among the primes. Strained book-to-bill ratios signal that the existing defense industrial base is consistently operating under strain, which is not the case across the broader commercial industrial base (Figure 5C a p a c i t y c o n s t r a i n t s n o t a b l e a m o n g t h e p r i m e s ). Limited labor pools, single-point suppliers, and the need for long lead items translate into rising backlogs that indicate demand is outpacing available productive capacity. In a system optimized for reliability and predictability rather than volatility and surge, this is a warning sign: “surge” is not a switch to be flipped, but a capability that must be cultivated and maintained. records.text: 7 June 2026 Metals & Mining Metals & Mining Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG have more than doubled over the past 12 months and are now pricing in a long-term aluminium price of ~$3,400/t. Iron ore: margins hit multi-year lows as costs bite Spot EBITDA margins for the iron ore majors (RIO, BHP, Vale) have fallen to their lowest levels since 2018, driven by weaker prices, sharply higher freight rates and rising operating costs. The current CFR 62% Fe iron ore price of ~$101/t is equivalent to a pre-war price of <$93/t for Australian producers. Margin pressure is more acute for higher-cost producers, although the upper end of the cost curve (> $100/t) should limit further downside. The weaker margin outlook may weigh on the majors following recent share price strength, alongside our high-frequency data pointing to a softer market. Separately, the Simandou project in Guinea is showing early signs of ramp up with reported shipments of 2.2 mt in May, up from 1.3 mt in April (refer to our report for details). Week ahead Vale is hosting a site visit to its Voisey's Bay mine and Long Harbour Processing Plant in Canada on 8-10 June. records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 08 June 2026 3 A 10% rise in oil prices lifts gasoline prices from the following month. Electricity follows with a lag of about six months. The effect likely begins to build after around three months, but in our analysis appears only after six months, reflecting the large weight of LNG and the use of multi-year contracts. By contrast, ex-energy BoJ core CPI rises more gradually. The impact peaks about one year after the shock and then persists at a similar pace for roughly another year. Lessons from the 2022 Ukraine shock The pattern is consistent with the 2022–23 inflation episode following the Ukraine shock. Import prices had already been rising since 2021, reflecting the post-COVID rebound in energy demand and supply-chain disruptions. The Ukraine shock added further pressure. CPI rose with a lag. Japan core CPI (ex. fresh food) peaked a little above 4% yoy in November 2022, while BoJ core CPI (ex. fresh food and energy) peaked at a similar level in Apr–Jun 2023, more than a year after the shock (Exhibit 4). We believe the main argument for eventual tightening will be an assessment that the Fed’s policy stance is miscalibrated. records.text: Top Projects 2026: PM Summary This 23rd edition of our annual review of top assets in global Oil & Gas production indicates a technological shift towards the main beneficiaries of AI and Digitalization in an effort to rebuild the industry’s reserve life: Deepwater exploration (better seismic imaging) and the globalisation of shale (drilling efficiency). We highlight five key themes of change vs. last year, and flag 15 companies with superior growth and profitability from their Top Projects portfolios: Top Projects oil reserve life is down 60% over a decade, while the market is now rewarding longer-life portfolios The resource life of Top Projects (recoverable resources/production) has fallen to c.20 years in 2026E from c.55 years in 2012, a 60% decrease over the past decade. However, we are starting to see a major shift and after years of demanding capital discipline since 2014, the market is now rewarding companies that reinvest and hold longer reserve life, with higher-reinvestment companies outperforming peers by c.20pp over the past 6 months (correlation r = +0.80, the strongest since the early 2000s commodity boom). In June, it might tweak the message just slightly by characterising inflation risks as more balanced, but we do not expect it to indicate that the policy outlook is tilted towards rate hikes. At the time of writing, the market is pricing 13bp of hikes by end-2026 and 35bp of hikes by September 2027. Recap: SNB message in March was for unchanged rates In March, the SNB kept the policy rate at 0%. Two aspects stood out to us. First, the SNB strengthened its language on FX interventions by saying its "willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market has increased" to counter "a rapid and excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc, which would jeopardise price stability in Switzerland." We estimate that the SNB indeed intervened in March, purchasing FX worth CHF 2.5bn but did not continue purchases in a meaningful way in April. Second, the inflation forecast was raised for the near-term, but slightly lowered for the medium-term. The message from both FX purchases and the inflation forecast, in our view, is that the SNB seems more worried about too low inflation (triggered by a strong CHF) than about high inflation (triggered by high oil prices). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 On this score, we think it's instructive to consider what happened in 2021, the last time the Fed was challenged with rising headline inflation, but core remained low enough for the Fed to look past what it thought was transitory drivers (mostly COVID supply chain disruptions). This time, it's energy spikes from the war and perhaps chipflation from the AI buildout. In 2021, earnings growth and inflation were booming but with the Fed on hold, stocks did well. Sound familiar? The question now is can the Fed continue to downplay the inflation risks and stay on hold? Given new chair Warsh's comments around AI as a potential productivity booster, we think the Fed will lean on the accommodative side at least through the mid-terms. This is exactly what the Fed did in 2021 until they could no longer ignore inflationary pressures. Exhibit 10 looks at this inflation analog alongside the 1970s. The comparison is worth noting in the sense that a double spike occurred as the Fed didn't fully extinguish the inflation risk initially (the Fed and most other central banks have missed their inflation targets for over 5 years). Notice how headline CPI is exactly where it was in April 2021. Is history repeating or at least rhyming? At the five-year horizon, a shorter time series, inflation expectations were unchanged at 3.0% in May. Overall, this survey suggests that inflation expectations remain well-anchored. One-year ahead inflation expectations can be sensitive to changes in gasoline prices, and the US average all-grade retail gasoline price rose to $4.61 at the end of May, up from $3.07 at the end of February. Despite the elevated level, one-year ahead inflation expectations fell 0.1 pp to 3.5% in May, now 0.5 pp above the February level prior to the conflict. Gas price expectations also eased slightly. The year-ahead gas price change expectation fell 0.1 pp to 5.0% in May, remaining well above the 3.7% average in the 12 months prior to the conflict and the 2.7% level in May a year ago. Labor market expectations were mixed in May. The mean probability of leaving one's job voluntarily rose 2.6 pp to 20.8%, a post-pandemic high. Program Cost The F-35’s performance ambitions have been accompanied by persistent scrutiny over cost growth and schedule pressure. Total lifetime program costs are estimated to exceed $2.1 trillion through an expected horizon extending to 2088, with a per-aircraft cost cited at approximately $90 million. The most consequential driver, however, is sustainment – an estimated 75% of total costs accrue from operations, maintenance, and repairs, underscoring that the program’s long-run economics are dominated by readiness, supply chain performance, and depot capacity rather than procurement alone. For example, program costs increased from about $1.1 trillion in 2018 to $1.58 trillion 2023—a 44% increase—which was attributed to the compounding burden of a complex global supply chain and the logistics required to maintain availability over time. Challenges faced in a future war with a peer adversary Despite its advanced technology and central role in U.S. force planning, the F-35 has clear liabilities in a peer conflict defined by A2/AD threats, long distances, and heavy electronic/cyber contestation—with direct operational and industrial-base implications. records.text: 1 Insights Classification: ComplimentaryMaterial ECB Preview: Insurance hike or a new cycle? 9 June 2026 With the ECB set to restart its hiking cycle this week, the policy decision itself is unlikely to surprise. Markets have consistently leaned toward a hike since prior to the April meeting, with at least 18bps priced from April 20, now rising to a full 25bps in OIS—effectively a done deal. That said, there will still be meaningful signals to extract, particularly from the updated staff projections. In March, the ECB presented three scenarios—baseline, adverse, and severe—and current conditions appear to sit somewhere between the baseline and adverse cases. While gas prices have tracked closer to the baseline, oil has behaved more in line with the adverse scenario, which assumed a peak around $119/bbl. Relative to the baseline, the adverse scenario implied inflation would be 0.9ppt higher in 2026 and modestly higher into 2027 (+0.1ppt). Current inflation swap pricing suggests expectations are modestly above the baseline in the near term, before converging to a less elevated path by 2027 (Figure 1). At the last meeting President Lagarde indicated that a key to the path forwards will hinge on second round effects, holding that as of the April meeting, she was not seeing second round effects. However, observable cap rates reported in the CMBS conduit market expanded by less than 1%, resulting in much more stable pricing than anticipated (Figure 8). One reason that cap rates remained sticky is that CRE owners chose to hold onto their properties, in spite of the theoretical loss of value. In most cases, this made good business sense, as the underlying properties continued to perform well. Most loans that were outstanding at the time benefited from conservative post-COVID underwriting, with L TVs in the low 50% range and healthy debt service coverage ratios well exceeding 2x. Further, most CRE loans are either fixed-rate or contain rate caps, so borrowing costs did not soar as rates rose. In our view, this gives the BoC scope to remain patient while earlier policy easing continues to feed through (Figure 1). The more encouraging news is that signs of recovery are emerging in Q2. Statistics Canada’s advance estimate points to 0.4% GDP growth in April. Retail sales rose for a fourth straight month through April, while the unemployment rate fell in May to its lowest level since January. The three-month moving average of job gains is also the strongest since November (Figure 2). At the same time, three-month annualized core inflation has remained contained at 1.8%, although it has been edging higher alongside headline inflation (Figure 3). Taken together, these trends give the BoC room to stay on hold and assess how the economy develops in the near term. Our Hawkish-Dovish Index ranks Canada as the most dovish central bank in the G10 (Figure 4). Combined with the significant uncertainty surrounding the USMCA review beginning on July 1, this leads us to downgrade our CAD view from positive to neutral until there is greater clarity. Even so, we believe the recovery is taking hold and that much of the bad news is already priced in, which keeps us from turning short the CAD at current levels. But it is used to supplement more exquisite systems with cheap munitions used in large scale attrition attacks such as for drone warfare. Barracuda is purpose-built to bring mass to the fight. Designed from the ground-up for hyper-scale manufacturing, its production rates can be doubled on-call to meet short-term surges in demand. Barracuda is designed to be simple to manufacture, both in terms of tooling and talent. records.text: Michael Metcalfe, Caroline Coughlin 08 June 2026 US inflation : Higher for longer? The first and third largest monthly jumps in the State Street PriceStats index in March and April matched subsequent reported moves in the Bureau of Labour Statistics (BLS) data almost exactly; an average of error of a couple of basis points is small when compared to large one percentage point jumps. If such a close relationship holds for May, we can expect more disappointing news on headline inflation (Figure 1). State Street PriceStats rose ‘only’ 0.65 percent month-over-month increase in inflation (NSA) on the month. This is half the monthly rate of inflation seen in March, and a third lower than the rise in April. But it is still a significant monthly rise. Prior to March and April, such a reading would have been the highest monthly reading since June 2022; the peak of the last inflation shock. The message is that inflation momentum slowed in May, but it is still strong. This has pushed the annual inflation rate up even higher, after climbing past 4 percent at the end of March ; the annual inflation rate according to State Street PriceStats, rose above 5 percent at the end of May (Figure 2). The official inflation rate, which jumped 4.1 percent excluding shelter in April, appears to have potential to rise even further. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear A growing theme in FX is the policy divergence among central banks. As such, it is worth exploring how the pricing of Fed hikes compares with market expectations for other central banks. Since the start of the Middle East conflict, global front- end yields have risen to reflect the upside risks to inflation from higher energy prices. If there is a resolution to the conflict soon, we think Fed hike pricing will be more durable than the expectations of hikes from other central banks, as the Fed repricing was driven by stronger activity data, while central bank repricing elsewhere was driven by energy prices. Thus, if a de-escalation contributes to broad USD weakness, we could see it as a selective ‘buy the dip’ opportunity in the USD, as rate differentials may move in favour of the dollar. When deciding where to buy the dip, we think buying the USD against low yielders would be favourable as markets would seek to earn carry. We therefore think two conditions should be met in choosing a pair: ▪ the market should be pricing in hikes from the other currency’s central bank; and ▪ it should be unlikely that those hikes are ultimately delivered. USDCAD stands out here in that regard given the softer growth and steady inflation data in Canada. Ultimately, implementation is where reform succeeds or stalls, and where resistance is strongest. Institutional inertia, compliance culture, and legacy incentives slow progress. Structural barriers like budget categories and documentation requirements, plus the tendency to revert to familiar processes, further impede change. Political concerns about oversight can also limit flexibility. Without real follow-through that transforms day-to- day budgeting and execution, the commercial-first, software-centric agenda risks stalling not in law, but in the practical mechanics of funding, contracting, and acquisition incentives. Spending-to-GDP levels have been roughly flat versus 2024 – the lower budget deficit is being achieved through higher taxes. The absence of a parliamentary majority has made it difficult to pursue a de-indexation of spending from inflation over the past two years. We think it will likely be politically even harder at a time of elevated inflation. 2027 budget hurdles look larger: Compared to last year, there is a low probability that a compromise to pass the 2027 budget will be found, with discussions set to take place just a few months before the presidential election. Private REITs also draw from retail investors and experienced heavy redemptions from late 2022 to early 2024. records.text: Meeting, requests from market participants varied widely, from accelerating the reduction to continuing it or halting it, with the latter being a minority view. In such circumstances, if the BoJ decides to halt the reduction, it will be accompanied by a responsibility to provide a very thorough explanation. A decision to halt the reduction can find its own economic rationale. This is because, in a rate hike phase, curbing excessive rises in long-term interest rates and heightened volatility can be considered a legitimate policy objective to ensure financial market stability. However, the timing is the problem. Amid media reports suggesting the government would condone a rate hike on the condition that the BoJ halts the reduction of its JGB purchases (e.g., Nikkei on May 28, TV Tokyo's "Morning Satellite" on June 4), a simultaneous decision to raise rates and halt the reduction could, regardless of its true intent, be perceived by the market and the public as a "political deal with the government." This carries a serious risk of creating doubts about the BoJ's independence, which is the cornerstone of monetary policy credibility. Thus, while halting the reduction of JGB purchases has the legitimate objective of "market stabilization," a simultaneous decision with a rate hike presents a dilemma with the serious side effect of "doubts about independence." ENI has also been able to successfully translate exploration activities into valuable giant oil and gas discoveries. Over the last five years, ENI has made a number of giant discoveries including: Zohr in Egypt; Mamba-Coral, Agulha in Mozambique; Mexico Area 1 in Mexico; and several oil discoveries in Block 15-06 in Angola. We assess the industry’s ability to create value through exploration by calculating the current NAV of the reserves accessed by each company over the past 10 years; in the exhibits below, we only show the top companies in terms of value added. The Ukraine conflict has massively accelerated these trends, making clear that operational advantage now flows from the ability to connect sensors and shooters, maintain decision superiority under attack, and rapidly regenerate combat power despite attrition. Additionally, U.S. forces face increasing challenges from adversaries pursuing Anti- Access/Area-Denial (A2/AD) strategies, particularly exemplified by China. These adversaries contest forward bases, threaten concentrated formations, and deny access to critical maritime and air corridors, pushing U.S. doctrine toward distributed operations, longer-range effects, and dynamic force employment. In other words, this is a strategy designed to make it hard for an opponent to get into a region (“anti-access”) and hard for them to operate effectively once they’re there (“area denial”). It’s a playbook for turning a contested zone into a place where enemy forces can’t safely arrive, can’t communicate well, can’t see clearly, and can’t move or fight freely. It typically combines tools like electronic warfare (jamming), cyber attacks, long-range missiles, and advanced air defenses to disrupt communications and sensing, threaten ships and aircraft from far away, and raise the cost and risk of operating near the contested area.
